content: The air in the Blackridge Data Vault didn’t breathe—it *hummed*: a low, relentless thrum from ten thousand servers, vibrating up through the perforated steel floor into my soles like the pulse of something vast and indifferent. Flickering emergency LEDs cast jagged, blood-orange slashes across endless aisles of black server racks, their blinking eyes cold and unblinking as a morgue fridge. My trench coat smelled of rain-slicked asphalt and cheap synth-whiskey; the only warmth came from the heat-sink vents exhaling dry, metallic breath against my neck. A single terminal glowed in the gloom—*access denied* in harsh crimson letters—and beside it, a discarded thumb drive lay on the cold floor, its casing cracked, a thin smear of something dark and viscous—oil? blood?—glistening under the emergency light. I picked it up. Cold. Heavy. Like holding a dead man’s last secret. Somewhere deep in the server farm, a rack alarm began to whine—not loud, not urgent, just a thin, dying insect buzz. Then it cut out. Silence rushed back in, thicker now, heavier, and I knew, with the hollow certainty that only comes when the lights flicker *just* long enough for the shadows to swallow your reflection in the black glass of a dead monitor, that I wasn’t alone. And whatever had been watching hadn’t blinked.
